aka: Ajinomoto Build-up Film, build-up film, ABF build-up film, ABF substrate, ABF substrates
plain: The insulating film inside the base board, the substrate, that every high-end chip package sits on. The board is built up in layers, and a sheet of this epoxy film, about 10 micrometers thick, separates each layer of copper wiring from the next. The Japanese food company Ajinomoto developed it out of its amino acid chemistry.
why: Every high-end CPU, GPU and AI accelerator sits on a substrate built from it. Ajinomoto puts its own share at about 95 percent, so a shortage of this one film would stop accelerators shipping.

aka: AI accelerator, XPU, accelerators
plain: A chip built to do the one kind of arithmetic machine learning needs, multiplying large grids of numbers, far faster than a general-purpose processor can. Nvidia's graphics processors, Google's Tensor Processing Units and Amazon's Trainium are all accelerators.
why: Accelerators are what the whole supply chain is for, and the unit that export licenses are granted or refused for.

aka: 2.5D packaging, 3D packaging, 2.5D, 2.5D work, advanced packaging plants
plain: The steps that assemble several finished chips into one component, sitting side by side or stacked, wired together closely enough to behave like a single larger chip. Ordinary packaging only puts one chip into a protective case with contacts on the bottom.
why: An AI accelerator is too large to print as one chip, and its memory must sit beside the logic, so every one is assembled this way. It capped AI chip output in 2025.

aka: atomic layer deposition
plain: A way of coating a chip roughly one atomic layer at a time. Each pulse of gas sticks to the surface and then stops once the surface is covered, so the film ends up the same thickness on the floor and on the walls of a hole hundreds of times deeper than it is wide.
why: Atomic layer deposition is what makes stacked memory and wrap-around transistors possible, and US export rules name it directly. It is the one tool category where Chinese suppliers still hold under 1 percent of the market.

aka: application-specific integrated circuit, custom silicon, ASICs, custom accelerator, custom accelerators, custom chip, custom AI silicon, custom AI ASICs
plain: A one-customer chip, designed for a single job and never sold on the open market. Google's Tensor Processing Unit and Amazon's Trainium are chips of this kind; an Nvidia part sold to any customer is not.
why: Custom chips are how the largest cloud buyers try to escape Nvidia's pricing, and roughly 95 percent of the work of designing them alongside the buyer runs through just two firms, Broadcom and Marvell.

aka: automated test equipment, tester
plain: The machine that connects to a finished chip, feeds it millions of test patterns and checks whether the answers coming back are right. It is the only stage of chip manufacturing that runs electricity through the product.
why: An AI accelerator joins a dozen expensive pieces, and one bad piece scraps them all, so each die is tested first. Advantest and Teradyne hold about 80 percent of the tester market.

aka: ball grid array, FC-BGA, flip-chip BGA
plain: A way of joining a packaged chip to a circuit board using a grid of small solder balls across the underside in place of a row of pins around the edge. Heating the assembly melts every ball at once into a permanent joint.
why: The number and spacing of those balls limit how much current and how many signals can reach a package, which matters when a single AI accelerator draws more than a thousand amps.

aka: BOM
plain: The itemized list of every purchased part in a finished product and what each part cost, the way a builder's invoice prices lumber, wiring and fixtures separately.
why: On an AI accelerator the memory line alone is roughly half of manufacturing cost, so the bill of materials shows which suppliers capture the money a buyer spends.

aka: Bureau of Industry and Security, part of the US Department of Commerce
plain: The US government office that decides which technologies may be exported, to whom, and on what conditions. It writes the rules, issues the licenses and brings the enforcement cases.
why: Almost every restriction on selling AI chips or chipmaking tools to China is a bureau rule, and the bureau can change a threshold with a Federal Register notice, with no act of Congress needed.

aka: capital expenditure, capital spending
plain: Money a company spends on long-lived physical assets such as buildings, machines and servers, as distinct from salaries and other running costs.
why: It buys the chips, racks and buildings, so the largest cloud companies' capex sets demand for the whole chain. The five largest spent $448.3 billion in 2025, and on that trend reach $770 billion in 2026.

aka: chiplets
plain: One of several smaller pieces that a chip has been deliberately split into, each manufactured separately and then wired back together inside a single package. A chip built this way is a house assembled from prefabricated rooms.
why: An AI accelerator needs more circuit than one exposure can print, so modern accelerators are built from chiplets. That moves the hard part into packaging, which capped AI chip output through 2024 and 2025.

aka: chokepoints
plain: A step in the supply chain where so few firms or countries can do the work that losing one of them stops everybody. The term comes from Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, which mapped the chip industry segment by segment to find the ones with only one or two suppliers.
why: Chokepoints are where a policy has effect, and where one sanction or one factory fire reaches the whole industry.

aka: training compute threshold
plain: A limit set on the amount of arithmetic used to train an AI model. It counts operations, whichever chips run them. The 2023 US executive order on AI set its reporting line at "any model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations" (Executive Order 14110, section 4.2(b)(i), 88 FR 75191). The same number became an export control in January 2025: ECCN 4E091 covers "'Parameters' for an artificial intelligence model trained utilizing 10^26 or more 'operations'", and 15 CFR 742.6(a)(13) requires a license for them to every destination worldwide. Europe drew its line ten times lower, at a cumulative training run "greater than 10^25" floating point operations, in Article 51(2) of the EU AI Act.
why: Every other control threshold measures a chip. This one measures the model the chips train, which is the only place the rules reach a capability itself. The two numbers also disagree by a factor of ten, and Article 51(3) lets the European Commission move its figure by delegated act, so the model-level line is the one most likely to shift.

aka: concentration band
plain: A four-band judgment of how many firms could credibly supply a stage today, taken at the narrowest step inside it. Extreme means three or fewer, or one firm holding more than half the stage. High means four to six, with the top two taking most of the revenue. Moderate means seven or more, none of them dominant. Low means many, with the scarce input something another industry sells at volume. Where a figure exists for the top country's share of the segment, it serves as a second check, and the supplier count wins when the two disagree.
why: The fewer the firms that can do a stage, the more one accident or one license decision moves the whole chain.

aka: Country Group, Country Group D:5, D:5, A:5, D:1, D:3, D:4, arms-embargoed countries
plain: The groups that US export rules sort the world's countries into, published as supplement no. 1 to 15 CFR part 740. A:5 and A:6 are close partners; D:1, D:4 and D:5 are the national security, missile technology and arms-embargoed groups; E:1 and E:2 are the most restricted. A country can sit in several at once, and the license requirement usually turns on which.
why: The license rule for AI chips is written in country groups: a license is needed for D:1, D:4 and D:5 destinations that are not also A:5 or A:6 (15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)). Moving the UAE into A:5 in July 2026 changed its position without naming it in the rule.

aka: chip on wafer on substrate
plain: TSMC's method for mounting logic chips and memory stacks side by side on a shared slab of silicon, then mounting that slab on a rigid base board. Nearly every high-end AI accelerator is built this way.
why: CoWoS capacity was the practical ceiling on AI accelerator output through 2025, and Nvidia has booked more than half of TSMC's 2026 to 2027 expansion.

plain: The share of controlled American content a foreign-made item may contain before US export rules, the EAR, apply to it. Under 15 CFR 734.4 the general threshold is 25 percent of the item's value, and 10 percent for the most restricted destinations. Above the line the item is caught; below it, it is not.
why: It is the ordinary way an item leaves American jurisdiction, and the reason the foreign direct product rules were written: those rules ignore the percentage altogether. There is no de minimis at all for the advanced-node equipment named in 15 CFR 734.4(a)(3).

aka: D0, defects per square centimeter
plain: The average number of chip-killing flaws per square centimeter of processed wafer. It is a fab's quality score, inferred from how many chips come out working.
why: AI accelerators have the largest dies in production, and yield falls steeply with die area times defect density. On an 8 square centimeter die, halving defect density lifts yield from about 49 to about 69 percent.

plain: An order from BIS that shuts a named party out of trade in US-controlled items, as a penalty. It is a punishment, and no license policy is involved. Under 15 CFR 764.3 it suspends or revokes the party's outstanding licenses and bars exports, reexports and in-country transfers of any item subject to the EAR to or by that party. There is no application to file. Orders can be issued outright or suspended and later activated.
why: It is the only instrument that stops trade absolutely. The order activated against ZTE in April 2018 halted most of the company's production within weeks and was terminated 89 days later on settlement (83 FR 17644; 83 FR 34825).

plain: Adding a layer of material to a wafer, either by knocking atoms off a solid target so they land on the surface, or by reacting gases at the surface so a film grows there. It is how the insulators, the wires and the parts of each transistor are built up.
why: A chip takes more than a thousand rounds of deposition and etch, and AI hardware needs films that reach the bottom of deeper holes. Four firms make most of the tools, and Chinese toolmakers are strongest here.

aka: singular of dice, dies
plain: One rectangular chip cut out of a wafer. Hundreds are printed side by side on the same disc and then sliced apart, and each separated rectangle is a die.
why: Cost, yield and export thresholds are all reckoned per die, and AI accelerators use among the largest dies in production, which makes every defect far more expensive.

aka: dynamic random-access memory
plain: A computer's main working memory. Each bit is a charge held in a microscopic capacitor that leaks, so the whole chip has to be refreshed thousands of times a second and forgets everything when the power goes off.
why: HBM is a stack of DRAM chips, so only the three leading DRAM makers can build it. Every wafer they turn to HBM is one not making ordinary DRAM, which is how AI demand raises the price of a laptop.

aka: deep ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, DUV scanner, DUV scanners, DUV tools
plain: The older kind of chipmaking light, and the machines that print with it, which still make up most lithography tools. The light comes from gas lasers, at 248 or 193 nanometers. Filling the gap between lens and wafer with water sharpens the image, a method called immersion.
why: Without extreme ultraviolet, a fab reaches leading-edge logic only with immersion deep ultraviolet and several passes per layer, as SMIC does, so immersion is where Dutch export licensing draws its line.

aka: Export Administration Regulations
plain: The body of US rules that governs the export of commercial goods, software and technology, including items with both civilian and military uses, written and enforced by the Bureau of Industry and Security. They run from 15 CFR part 730 to part 774: part 734 sets what they cover, part 742 the license requirements, part 744 the end-use and end-user controls, part 740 the exceptions and part 764 the penalties.
why: Almost every American export rule on chips and chip tools amends these regulations. They are changed by a notice in the Federal Register, with no act of Congress, which is why a threshold can move in a week.

plain: The label for an item that falls under US export rules but is not named on the Commerce Control List, the catalog of controlled items, from 15 CFR 734.3(c). It is a residual category with conditions: an EAR99 item still needs a license if it is going to a listed party or a controlled end use.
why: Most of what a chip plant buys is EAR99. It is the answer to "do I need a license?" for the great majority of shipments, and the reason the end-user controls in part 744 matter more than the classification for many exporters.

aka: Export Control Classification Number
plain: The catalog number that US export rules assign to a controlled item, rather like a customs tariff code for security-sensitive technology. Number 3A090 covers advanced computing chips and 3B001 covers chipmaking equipment.
why: An item's classification number decides whether it needs a license, so the technical thresholds written into each number are where the policy takes effect.

aka: electronic design automation, chip design software
plain: The software that turns a description of what a chip should do into the exact pattern of shapes to be printed on silicon, and proves the result will work before anyone commits money to masks and wafers.
why: Three vendors sell every complete design flow used at the leading edge, which is why stopping their sale to China in May 2025 took three letters and no lead time.

aka: end user, end users, end-user, end use, military end user
plain: Export rules that turn on who the buyer is and what they will do with the item, whatever the item is. The same tool can ship freely to one customer and need a license that will be refused for another.
why: These controls reach past the product to the customer, so a company can lose access because of who owns it or what its site produces, as when US rules were extended to firms majority owned by listed entities.

aka: entity-list, Entity-Listed, Entity List additions, listed entity, listed entities, listed firm, listed firms
plain: A published list of foreign companies, institutes and individuals that need a license before anyone anywhere, American or foreign, may send them an item subject to the EAR. Each entry states its own license review policy, so a listing is not one uniform outcome: most carry a presumption of denial, meaning the license will normally be refused; SMIC's is case by case except for items uniquely capable of production at 10 nanometers and below. It is supplement no. 4 to 15 CFR part 744, and the license requirement is in 15 CFR 744.11.
why: The fastest and simplest instrument Washington has: it names an organization. Since September 2025 a listing has reached companies the listed firm half owns, though that extension is stayed to 9 November 2026 (90 FR 50857).

aka: etching, etched, etches, etcher, etchers, dry etch
plain: Removing material from a wafer wherever the printed pattern says it should not be, usually by turning a gas into a plasma whose ions and fragments eat one material while leaving the material beside it alone.
why: Stacked memory and wrap-around transistors need holes far deeper than they are wide, which is why US rules control etch tools by hole shape and selectivity.

aka: extreme ultraviolet, extreme-ultraviolet, EUV scanner, EUV scanners, extreme ultraviolet lithography
plain: The light that prints the finest layers of every leading-edge chip, and the machines that print with it. Its wavelength is 13.5 nanometers, and shorter light draws finer lines. Air and glass both absorb it, so the machine works in a vacuum and carries the light on mirrors. The light comes from droplets of molten tin, 50,000 a second, each hit twice by a laser.
why: The finest layers set how densely transistors and wires pack, so no leading-edge AI chip can be made without EUV. Only ASML makes the machines, and none has ever been sold to a customer in China.

aka: fabrication plant, wafer fab, fabs, chip factory, chip factories
plain: The factory where wafers are processed into chips. It is a cleanroom with a second building's worth of pumps, gas cabinets and water treatment underneath it, and a leading-edge one costs $15 to $25 billion and takes four to six years to build.
why: Fab construction is the slowest part of any reshoring plan and the one that needs the most capital, which is why subsidy programs on three continents target it and why the capacity they buy arrives late this decade.

plain: A chip company that designs and sells chips but owns no factory, paying a contract manufacturer, a foundry, to make them. Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm and Broadcom all work this way.
why: The fabless model concentrates manufacturing in a handful of foundries, so a designer's supply, cost and geographic exposure are set by a company it does not control.

aka: fin field-effect transistor
plain: A transistor whose channel, the strip that current flows through, is stood on edge like a shark fin, so that the gate, the electrode that switches the current, wraps around three of its sides instead of resting on one. More contact means firmer control and less leakage when the switch is meant to be off.
why: FinFET was the standard transistor shape from roughly 2011 until 2025, and US export rules still use 16 nanometer FinFET production as one threshold for what counts as an advanced fab.

aka: floating point operations per second, TFLOPS, PFLOPS, FLOP, teraflops
plain: A count of how many arithmetic operations on decimal numbers a chip can perform each second, the way horsepower counts an engine's output.
why: The standard unit of AI compute and the basis of export thresholds, but only comparable between chips when the number format behind it is stated.

aka: FDPR, FDP rule, foreign-produced direct product rule, direct product rule, foreign-produced item rules, foreign-produced item rule, foreign-produced item
plain: A US rule that puts a foreign-made item under American control when two tests are both met. The first is about the product: the item was made directly from specified US technology or software, or in a plant that was. The second is about the destination: the item is going somewhere, or to someone, the rule names. Both halves are needed. The mechanics are in 15 CFR 734.9.
why: The rule is what makes US controls extraterritorial. Without it a listed buyer could order the same chip from a supplier outside America; with it, a chip made in Taiwan on American tools for a listed Chinese firm needs a US license.

aka: pure-play foundry, contract chipmaker, foundries, pure-play, pure play, pure-play model, contract chipmaking
plain: A factory business that manufactures chips designed by other companies and promises never to compete with them. TSMC created the model in 1987, and it worked because no single design house sells enough chips to fill a modern fab.
why: TSMC took about 73 percent of foundry revenue in 2026 and nearly all leading-edge production, so one company's capacity plan sets the world's supply of AI chips.

aka: 8-bit and 4-bit floating point, FP8, FP4, FP16, BF16, INT8, number formats
plain: Ways of writing a number using only 8 or 4 binary digits, or bits, instead of the 32 a computer traditionally uses. Each number is less precise, but the chip can perform and store far more of them, which suits machine learning better than it would suit accounting.
why: Halving the precision roughly doubles a chip's headline speed, so a performance figure quoted without its number format is meaningless and an export threshold has to say which format it counts.

aka: GAA, nanosheet transistor, RibbonFET at Intel, nanosheet, nanosheets, RibbonFET, GAA transistor, gate-all-around transistors
plain: A transistor in which the gate, the electrode that switches the current, wraps all the way round the channel that current flows through; a fin's gate touches three sides. Surrounding the channel gives the gate full control, so the switch still turns fully off as dimensions shrink.
why: Only TSMC, Intel and Samsung can build the 2 nanometer generation's transistor in volume, and it is what drives new demand for atomic layer deposition and sideways etching tools.

aka: graphics processing unit, GPUs
plain: A processor originally built to draw video game images by doing thousands of simple calculations simultaneously. That same shape of arithmetic turned out to be what neural networks need, so this chip became the default AI processor.
why: Nvidia holds roughly 70 percent of the AI chip market, and its graphics processors are what most export licenses name.

plain: The share of a sale left over after paying what it cost to make the thing, before research, sales and overheads are counted. A 70 percent gross margin means $70 of every $100 of revenue survives manufacturing cost.
why: Gross margin shows where pricing power sits: chip designers, memory makers and inspection-tool vendors keep well over half of each sale, substrate makers about a third, and assembly and test houses under a fifth.

aka: high bandwidth memory, high-bandwidth memory, HBM3E, HBM4, HBM4E, HBM stack, HBM stacks, memory stacks, stacked memory
plain: Stacked memory built for AI chips. Up to sixteen memory chips are stacked into a cube, wired together by copper that runs straight down through them, and the cube sits a few millimeters from the processor. It holds the model the chip is running, the numbers called weights, and hands them to the processor over 1,024 or more wires at once.
why: To write each word of an answer, the chip reads the whole model from this memory, along with the record of the conversation so far. A larger model or a longer conversation needs more memory, so the size and speed of HBM usually set how many people one chip can serve. It is the most expensive part of an AI accelerator, and only SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make it.

aka: high numerical aperture extreme ultraviolet, ASML EXE series, High-NA, High NA, High-NA scanners, High-NA machine, High-NA tools
plain: The next generation of extreme ultraviolet machine, whose larger mirrors collect light over a wider angle and so print smaller features. The wider optics also halve the area the machine can print in one exposure, so a large chip has to be stitched together from two exposures.
why: It cuts the smallest printable feature from 13 nanometers to 8, and TSMC expects more AI chip layers to need it. Each machine costs $350 to $400 million. Intel uses it in volume now, and TSMC plans to from 2030.

aka: direct bond interconnect, SoIC, Foveros, copper pad to copper pad
plain: Joining two chips face to face by pressing their copper pads, and the glass-like insulator around them, into direct contact, with no solder in between. Removing the solder lets connections be packed much more tightly and shortens the path heat has to travel out.
why: Taller, cooler memory stacks depend on this step, only two suppliers make the tools, and every slip in their schedule moves the memory roadmap with it.

aka: hyperscalers
plain: One of the handful of companies that run data centers at global scale and buy computing hardware by the gigawatt: Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and, on most definitions, Oracle.
why: They pay for the AI buildout, $448.3 billion of capital at the five largest in 2025, committed years before the hardware exists.

aka: integrated device manufacturer, integrated device maker, integrated device makers
plain: A chip company that both designs its products and manufactures them in its own factories. Intel, Samsung and Micron are the main surviving examples.
why: An integrated maker that also rents out factory capacity is competing with its own customers, which is the commercial reason Intel and Samsung struggle to win other firms' flagship designs.

aka: transfer (in-country)
plain: A change in the end use or the end user of an item inside one foreign country, defined at 15 CFR 734.16. Nothing crosses a border: a server legally imported into a country for one customer is transferred when it is resold, or repurposed, for another.
why: It is the step that catches hardware diverted after it has landed, and it is why a license granted for a named Chinese customer does not travel with the hardware. Reexports and in-country transfers of advanced chips to Country Group D:5 keep a presumption of denial even where an export would be read case by case (91 FR 1685).

aka: interposers, silicon interposer, silicon carrier
plain: A slab of silicon carrying wiring but no transistors, used as a miniature circuit board underneath several chips so they can be connected at a density no ordinary board could reach.
why: HBM connects over 1,024 or 2,048 wires, too many for a resin board, so memory and logic sit together on an interposer. Its area caps how much fits in one package, now 5.5 times the reticle.

aka: is informed letter, is-informed letters, by letter
plain: A letter from BIS to one named company imposing a license requirement on a specific export, without any rule being published. The authority is written into the regulations themselves, for example 15 CFR 744.23(b), which lets BIS inform a person individually, with no amendment to the EAR.
why: It is the fastest way a control is imposed. The A100 and H100 requirement of August 2022 and the H20 requirement of April 2025 both arrived this way, and the public learned of each from the company's own filing.

aka: KGD, good die, good dies, known good die
plain: A bare chip tested thoroughly enough, before assembly, to be trusted inside something expensive. In an ordinary product a faulty chip wastes one chip; inside a stacked package it can ruin thirty.
why: As packages grow toward ten logic chips and twenty memory stacks, the cost of catching a bad one late pushes testing and burn-in, running chips hot to force early failures, back onto the wafer.

aka: license exception
plain: A written carve-out in export rules that lets a shipment go without an individual license, if it meets stated conditions. The ones that matter for AI chips are NAC and ACA (15 CFR 740.8), HBM (740.25), AIA and LPP, which carry the top band of accelerators to allies and in small volumes elsewhere (740.27 and 740.29), IEC for allied countries that adopt matching controls (740.24), and RPL for servicing and spare parts (740.10).
why: Exceptions are how a control regime is tuned without rewriting it, and how Washington rewards allies: License Exception IEC, added in September 2024, is open only to countries that have imposed equivalent national controls (89 FR 72926).

aka: ACA, Advanced Computing Authorized
plain: An export rule that lets AI chips below the top band ship to most of the world with no license and no advance notice. It covers the same chips as its companion exception NAC, and every destination except Macau and Country Group D:5. The top-band data center chips in ECCN 3A090.a are excluded and need a license to any destination. It was added to 15 CFR 740.8 in December 2024.
why: It lets chips below the top band reach most of the world with no paperwork, while NAC keeps a notice requirement for Macau and D:5. Before December 2024 NAC did both jobs, so an older table that shows one exception describes what is now two.

plain: An export rule that lets high bandwidth memory reach a packaging plant in China with no license, to be packaged beside a chip. The chip's designer must buy the memory, the exporter must be headquartered in the United States or Country Group A:5, and the stacks must go straight to the packaging site. Inside China the rule covers co-packaging only below a memory bandwidth density of 3.3 GB/s per square millimeter. It sits at 15 CFR 740.25.
why: It keeps Chinese packaging houses in the supply chain of American and allied chip designers, while the same stacks may not be sold to a Chinese customer. HBM needs a license only for Macau and Country Group D:5, and the exception was written into the December 2024 rule that first controlled HBM (89 FR 96790).

aka: LPP, Low Processing Performance
plain: An export rule that lets a buyer almost anywhere receive a capped amount of top-band AI chips each year without a license. The cap is 26,900,000 TPP, the export rules' measure of computing power, per final recipient per year. Macau, Country Group D:5 and firms headquartered in either are excluded, and it does not cover transfers within a country. The AI Diffusion rule created it in January 2025, at 15 CFR 740.29.
why: It lets buyers outside the nineteen favored allies take top AI chips in small amounts with no license application. BIS said in May 2025 that it would not enforce the AI Diffusion rule, but it withdrew none of the text, so LPP still stands in the regulations beside AIA, ACM and the nineteen-country list.

aka: NAC, Notified Advanced Computing
plain: An export rule that lets AI chips below the top band ship to Macau and Country Group D:5, and to firms headquartered there, with no license, if the exporter tells BIS in advance and BIS does not object. The top-band data center chips in ECCN 3A090.a and the memory in 3A090.c are excluded. It sits at 15 CFR 740.8.
why: It is the one route for these chips into the restricted destinations that needs no license application. Since December 2024 the section carries two exceptions, NAC for the restricted destinations and ACA for everywhere else.

aka: direct-to-chip cooling, cold plate cooling, cold plate, cold plates, liquid-cooled, direct-to-chip liquid, direct liquid cooling
plain: Taking heat out of a processor by pumping water through a metal plate bolted directly onto it, instead of blowing air across a finned heatsink. Water carries far more heat per unit of volume, which is the only practical way to cool a rack drawing over a hundred kilowatts.
why: Every new AI hall is now plumbed for it, and an air-cooled hall cannot host an NVL72 rack without a full mechanical retrofit. It adds 7 to 10 percent to construction cost but cuts the floor area needed per megawatt by 70 to 85 percent.

aka: photolithography
plain: Printing a circuit pattern onto a wafer by shining light through a patterned plate and projecting a shrunken image of it onto a light-sensitive coating. It is photography at the scale of nanometers, repeated once for every layer of the chip.
why: The most concentrated stage in the chain, and the resolution a country can reach sets the ceiling on every chip it can make.

plain: The widening gap between how fast a processor can calculate and how fast memory can feed it numbers to work on. Computing speed has been roughly tripling every two years while memory bandwidth has less than doubled over the same period.
why: An AI chip reads its whole model from memory for each word it writes, so memory, more than arithmetic, now sets how fast it runs. The gap is why memory makes up nearly half the cost of an AI accelerator.

aka: process control, when grouped with inspection, metrology and inspection, inspection tools
plain: Measuring what a factory actually built: how wide a printed line came out, how thick a film is, whether this layer sits exactly on top of the last one. Inspection is the related job of finding flaws.
why: Without it a fab cannot find which of its steps is killing chips, so it cannot raise its yield, even if it has every other tool. One firm, KLA, holds about 57 percent of the market.

aka: double patterning, quadruple patterning, self-aligned quadruple patterning, multiple patterning, multi-patterning, several passes, several exposures, multiply exposed, DUV multipatterning
plain: Printing a single chip layer using two, three or four separate plates and etching steps, because one exposure cannot resolve features that close together. It is what a fab does when it cannot get sharper light.
why: China reaches advanced processes this way without extreme ultraviolet machines, taking roughly 34 lithography steps where nine would do, which is the direct source of its yield and cost penalty.

aka: process node, technology node, for example N2 or 18A, nodes
plain: The name a foundry gives one generation of its manufacturing process. The number in the name stopped measuring anything on the chip decades ago: nothing on TSMC's N2 is 2 nanometers wide, and SMIC's 5 nanometer-class process has a tighter metal spacing than Intel's 18A.
why: Because node names are marketing labels and measure nothing, rules and comparisons that rely on them are unreliable, which is why US export thresholds specify transistor type and metal spacing.

aka: GB200 NVL72, GB300 NVL72, Vera Rubin NVL72
plain: Nvidia's rack-sized product: 72 accelerators and 36 processors wired into one machine that software can treat as a single computer. The GB300 version draws up to 142 kilowatts.
why: AI capacity is now bought and priced by the rack, at roughly $5.0 million for a Grace Blackwell one and an estimated $7.8 million for its Vera Rubin successor.

aka: NVSwitch, NVLink 5, NVLink 6, NV-HBI
plain: Nvidia's private high-speed connection between its own accelerators, carrying up to 3,600 gigabytes per second per chip so that dozens of them can act as one. No other vendor sells a switch with comparable bandwidth.
why: A genuine single-vendor chokepoint inside an otherwise competitive systems layer, and the reason the rest of the industry created the UALink standard to compete with it.

aka: optical module, pluggable optics, optical transceivers, transceiver, transceivers, optical modules, 800G optical transceivers
plain: A small device that turns electrical signals into laser light for sending down a glass fiber, and turns them back at the far end. Every network link longer than a few meters in a large AI cluster needs one at each end.
why: A cluster needs several for each accelerator, 98,304 for 100,000 H100s. Chinese firms assemble the modules in volume, and only a few firms can make the lasers inside them, which is where supply runs short.

aka: outsourced semiconductor assembly and test, OSATs, outsourced assembly and test, assembly and test firms, assembly and test contractor, assembly and test houses
plain: A contract firm that takes finished wafers, cuts them into chips, seals the chips into packages and tests them. It is the back end of chipmaking, done for hire.
why: Every chip passes through assembly and test, and the work earns gross margins of only 17 to 21 percent. Its tools fall outside the export controls on lithography and deposition, so China is strongest here, with four of the ten largest firms.

aka: overlay error, alignment
plain: How precisely one printed layer of a chip lands on top of the layer beneath it. Before each exposure the scanner finds marks printed in earlier layers and lines the new layer up on them to within a few nanometers, across a disc 300 millimeters wide.
why: Misalignment can ruin whole regions of a wafer, so overlay is one of the specifications that separates an advanced printing machine from an ordinary one. Each extra pass on a layer is another chance to misalign.

aka: pellicles, EUV pellicle
plain: A thin transparent membrane held a few millimeters above a photomask so that dust settles on it, far enough out of focus that it does not print, and the pattern stays clean. It is a lens cap a photographer can shoot through.
why: No membrane yet survives extreme ultraviolet light while passing enough of it, so fabs trade printing speed against defect risk product by product, and solving this would cut the cost of that printing more than any machine upgrade.

plain: An export control test of how densely a chip packs its computing power. It divides the chip's TPP, the export rules' measure of computing power, by the area of its logic dies in square millimeters, memory stacks excluded, and applies only to a chip that already reaches 1,600 TPP. It replaced the 2022 test, which was based on interconnect bandwidth, the speed at which a chip exchanges data with its neighbors.
why: It closed the gap used by the A800 and H800, chips whose designers had tuned interconnect speed to fall under the 2022 threshold while keeping the compute. The line is now 1,600 TPP with a density of 5.92 (88 FR 73458).

aka: mask, reticle, mask set, photomasks, masks, mask sets, mask blank set
plain: The master template for one layer of a chip: a quartz plate, or for the shortest wavelengths a mirror, carrying the pattern that gets projected onto the wafer. A leading-edge chip needs seventy to a hundred of them, and the full set costs $10 million to $40 million.
why: Mask cost decides which chips can afford a leading-edge process at all, and the blank plates the masks are made from come from just two Japanese suppliers.

aka: resist, resists, EUV resist, EUV resists, resist makers
plain: The light-sensitive coating that records a chip's pattern during lithography. A machine spins a thin film of it across the wafer, light through a stencil changes the film where it lands, and a wash removes those parts, much like developing photographic film. What remains shows the next machine where to etch.
why: Every printed layer of a chip passes through it, and each formula is approved for one layer of one product at one fab, so switching supplier takes years. Japan made 78 percent of it in 2023, and a Japanese state-backed fund owns 84 percent of JSR, one of the largest makers.

plain: A license review policy. An application may be filed and will be considered, but the reviewing agencies start from the position that it should be refused, and the exporter has to overcome that. It is the policy for advanced computing chips going to China and Macau under 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10), and for most Entity List entries.
why: It is the distinction that decides whether a company files at all: under a presumption of denial an application can still be made, under a prohibition it cannot.

aka: probe cards
plain: A circuit board carrying thousands of fine needles that press down onto the contact pads of a chip while it is still part of the wafer, so a tester can drive signals into it. Every card is custom-built for one chip design.
why: Because cards are bespoke and slow to qualify, probe card supply and lead time set how fast a new accelerator or memory stack can ramp to volume.

aka: cabinet, racks, cabinets, rack-scale
plain: The standard steel frame that computing equipment is bolted into in a data center, roughly the size of a large refrigerator. AI systems have turned the rack from a container into the product, because an entire rack is now sold and wired as one machine.
why: Rack power went from about 120 kilowatts in 2024 to plans for a megawatt by 2027, and each step forces changes to cooling, busbars, floor loading and the substation outside.

plain: Shipping an item that falls under US export rules, the EAR, from one foreign country to another, defined at 15 CFR 734.14. A Korean stack of memory moving from Korea to China is a reexport, and it needs the same US license a shipment from Texas would.
why: Most of the trade the controls are aimed at never touches the United States. Without a rule on reexports, the controls would bind only American ports.

aka: photomask
plain: The patterned plate that a lithography machine projects onto the wafer, one chip layer at a time. In practice the word means the same as photomask, with reticle stressing that the machine steps the same image repeatedly across the disc.
why: The reticle's fixed printable area, 26 by 33 millimeters, is a hard physical limit that shapes how every large AI chip has to be designed.

aka: reticle size limit, reticle field, field size, reticle-limited, reticle size, reticles, times reticle
plain: The largest chip a lithography machine can print in a single exposure, about 858 square millimeters, or 26 by 33 millimeters. It is set by the machine's optics and is the same for every design.
why: Every AI accelerator worth buying is bigger than this, so designs must be split into chiplets and rejoined inside a package, which is how advanced packaging became the industry's bottleneck.

aka: back-end network, cluster fabric, scale-out, scale out
plain: The network that joins thousands of accelerator groups into one cluster, running at hundreds of gigabits per second over Ethernet or InfiniBand. The technology is ordinary data center networking; the scale is not.
why: It is how thousands of accelerators train one model together. Ethernet has overtaken InfiniBand here on raw capacity, moving the money to the switch chips Broadcom sells to all comers and to optical modules.

aka: scale-up fabric, coherent domain, scale-up, scale up, scale-up domain, scale-up switch
plain: The wiring that joins a few dozen accelerators inside one rack so a model too large for a single chip can be spread across them. It runs at terabytes per second, hundreds of times faster than the network between racks.
why: Scale-up bandwidth sets how large a model can be trained or served before the network becomes the limit, and Nvidia's NVLink is still the only product at the top of this market.

plain: The argument that Taiwan's dominance of advanced chipmaking deters an attack, because destroying or seizing TSMC would cost an aggressor and the world more than the island is worth.
why: The central and contested assumption behind Taiwan policy: a shield works only while it stays irreplaceable, which gives Taipei reason to slow the diversification its allies want.

aka: small yard with a high fence, small yard
plain: The stated design of US technology controls: restrict the narrow set of items that genuinely decide national security and leave the rest of the trade alone.
why: Whether the yard has stayed small is the standard test of whether export controls remain targeted security policy or have become general industrial policy.

plain: The test for whether an item falls under US export rules at all. Under 15 CFR 734.3 it covers anything in the United States, anything of US origin wherever it now sits, foreign-made goods that contain more than a permitted share of controlled US content, and foreign-made goods caught by a foreign direct product rule. Nationality of the seller is not the test; the item is.
why: The phrase decides who the rules apply to. A Dutch or Korean firm shipping between two foreign countries can still need a US license, because the rules follow the item.

aka: substitutability rating
plain: A four-band rating of how hard it would be for a well-funded state or firm, starting today, to build an alternative to the leaders of a stage, judged against four written tests. Easy: a second supplier is qualified, meaning approved by customers, and shipping today at the leading node, the most advanced process. Moderate: a second supplier exists but is not yet qualified at the leading node, about two to five years to close the gap. Hard: no second supplier at the leading node, five to ten years, and the path is known. Very hard: no second supplier, and the path runs through physics, decades of unwritten know-how or protected intellectual property, ten years or more, and nobody has repeated it yet. The clock always times the same actor and stops at qualification, well after a prototype.
why: It says how long a rival or a government would need to replace a stage, which is the question the export debate turns on.

aka: package substrate, IC substrate, substrates, build-up substrate, build-up substrates, package substrates, IC substrates, resin substrate
plain: The small, dense circuit board that a chip package sits on, spreading the chip's microscopic connections out to the millimeter-scale solder balls a motherboard can accept. It is built up layer by layer from epoxy film, laser-drilled holes and plated copper.
why: TSMC names substrates alongside memory as a limit on AI supply, and as packages grow, keeping a large one flat becomes harder than wiring it.

aka: tape out, taped out, tapes out, tape-outs, tapeout
plain: The moment a chip design is declared finished and the pattern files are sent to the factory to be written into masks. The name survives from when the data physically left on a reel of magnetic tape.
why: After tape-out any change costs a new mask set and a new manufacturing run, so it is the point where hundreds of millions of dollars of downstream commitment becomes irreversible.

aka: total processing performance
plain: The measure US export rules use for a chip's computing power: twice the number of multiply-accumulate operations, a multiply followed by an add, that it does each second, multiplied by the number of bits in each operation, added up across every processing unit on the chip. The definition sits in ECCN 3A090, in supplement no. 1 to 15 CFR part 774.
why: The dividing line for sales to China. Control starts at 4,800 TPP; since 15 January 2026 applications below 21,000 TPP and 6,500 GB/s of memory bandwidth are read case by case (91 FR 1685). Accelerators are now designed around the formula.

aka: Tensor Processing Unit, TPUs
plain: Google's own AI chip, designed in-house and used only inside Google's own data centers and cloud service. The seventh generation is called Ironwood.
why: The clearest evidence that a large buyer can build a real alternative to chips bought on the open market, with Google claiming a total cost per chip about 44 percent below that of the Nvidia server it replaces.

aka: transistors
plain: The switch every chip is built from. Current runs through a channel between two terminals, and a voltage on a third terminal, the gate, opens or closes that path much as a tap opens or closes a pipe. One Nvidia Blackwell part contains 208 billion of them.
why: Everything in this supply chain exists to make transistors smaller, faster and less leaky, and the difficulty of doing that is why the industry consolidated into so few firms.

aka: through-silicon via, TSVs, through-silicon vias, through silicon via, through silicon vias
plain: A copper column drilled all the way down through a chip so that power and signals can pass from its top face to its bottom face. It is what makes stacking chips vertically possible, in the way an elevator shaft makes a tall building usable.
why: These columns are what make high bandwidth memory possible, and US rules control the tools that cut them by hole shape and etching speed.

aka: Validated End-User, Validated End User, Validated End-User status, VEU status, VEU cover, validated end users
plain: An authorization BIS grants to a named foreign facility, letting approved items ship to it without an individual license each time. The approved facilities are listed in supplement no. 7 to 15 CFR part 748, and the procedure is 15 CFR 748.15.
why: It is what let Intel, Samsung and SK hynix run their fabs inside China on general authority after 2022. Revoking it in 2025 did not stop those fabs; it made every shipment a license application, and BIS said it would license operation but not expansion (90 FR 42321).

aka: silicon wafer, 300 mm wafer, wafers, silicon wafers, 300 mm wafers
plain: The polished disc of ultrapure silicon that chips are built on, 300 millimeters across and less than a millimeter thick. Hundreds of chips are printed on one disc and cut apart at the end.
why: A large AI die loses more silicon to each flaw, so AI chips need wafers nearly flawless and flat to the edge. Five firms supply the whole $11.4 billion market.

aka: WFE, front-end equipment, equipment billings, wafer processing equipment, semiconductor equipment, chipmaking tools, chipmaking equipment
plain: The collective name for the machines that process wafers inside a fab: printing systems, deposition and etch chambers, cleaning tools and measurement systems. It excludes the packaging and test machines used afterwards.
why: Spending on this equipment was a record $116.9 billion in 2025 and is the best early indicator of how much new chip capacity is being built, roughly two years before it produces anything.

aka: die yield, yields, packaging yield, package yield, stack yield
plain: The percentage of chips on a wafer that work. Flaws land at random, so the larger the chip the more likely it is to catch one, and yield falls steeply as chips get bigger.
why: Yield sets the cost of a working AI chip: a ten point yield drop on a reticle-sized die hurts far more than a 30 percent rise in the wafer price.

aka: chemical mechanical polishing, chemical mechanical planarization, polishing slurry, polishing slurries, slurry, slurries, CMP slurry, CMP pads, planarization
plain: After each new layer goes onto a wafer, its surface is rubbed flat again with a pad and a liquid full of fine grit, the slurry. The step is called chemical mechanical polishing, or CMP. Without it the next layer would be printed on a surface too bumpy to focus on.
why: A chip takes dozens of these polishes, and the slurry for each is qualified for one layer at one fab, which is why a $790 million slurry market has only two leaders.

aka: ion implanter, ion implanters, implant, implant layers, implantation
plain: A way of changing how silicon conducts by firing atoms into it. An ion implanter shoots charged atoms of boron, phosphorus or arsenic into the wafer so they lodge just under the surface, and the patches they land in conduct the way the design needs. It is the first step in building each transistor.
why: No transistor can be built without it. Implanters are export-controlled, and Applied Materials paid a $252 million penalty in 2026 for shipping them to a listed Chinese customer.

aka: epitaxial, epitaxial wafer, epitaxial wafers, epitaxial layer, epi
plain: Epitaxy grows a fresh layer of crystal on top of a wafer, atom by atom, so the new layer continues the crystal beneath it with almost no flaws. An epitaxial wafer is a plain wafer with that extra layer, and the transistors are built in that layer.
why: AI chips are built on epitaxial wafers because a big die cannot afford the defects a plain slice carries, which is where the wafer makers earn their money.

aka: polycrystalline silicon, electronic-grade polysilicon, semiconductor-grade polysilicon, polysilicon feedstock
plain: Polysilicon is silicon refined to purity but not yet grown into one crystal: gray rods made of many small crystals. It is the raw material that is melted down to pull the single crystal a wafer is cut from. The same material, at lower purity, goes into solar panels.
why: China makes about 93 percent of the world's polysilicon, but almost all of it is solar grade, so the dominance does not reach chips.

aka: electronic grade, semiconductor-grade, semiconductor grade, solar-grade, solar grade, eleven nines
plain: Electronic-grade silicon is pure enough for chips: fewer than one stray atom in a hundred billion, sometimes written as eleven nines. Solar-grade silicon is a thousand times dirtier, fine for a solar panel and useless for a transistor. The two grades come from different plants and different suppliers.
why: The line between the grades is the line between a Chinese commodity market and a German, American and Japanese one.

aka: immersion DUV, ArF immersion, immersion scanner, immersion scanners, immersion tools, immersion DUV scanners, immersion deep-ultraviolet
plain: An immersion scanner prints with a thin layer of ultrapure water between its lens and the wafer. Light bends more sharply through water than through air, so the same lens prints finer lines. It is the best that deep ultraviolet light can do, one step below extreme ultraviolet.
why: Immersion is the tier China can still buy and is now building itself, and it is where Dutch export licensing draws its line.

aka: argon fluoride, argon fluoride laser, 193 nm, 193-nanometer
plain: ArF is argon fluoride, the gas mixture inside the laser that gives deep ultraviolet scanners their 193-nanometer light. An ArF scanner, dry or immersion, prints most of the fine layers on any chip made without extreme ultraviolet.
why: ArF immersion was 42 percent of ASML's system sales in 2025, and it is the tier that China's domestic scanner effort is copying.

aka: krypton fluoride, krypton fluoride laser, 248 nm, 248-nanometer
plain: KrF is krypton fluoride, the gas in an older lithography laser that shines at 248 nanometers. KrF scanners print the coarser layers of a chip, where lines are far apart, and thick films for packaging.
why: Every chip still needs KrF layers, so the tool is in every fab, including China's, and nobody controls its export.

aka: g-line, i-line steppers, i-line scanners
plain: i-line is the coarsest lithography light still in use, 365 nanometers from a mercury lamp, named for one line in the lamp's spectrum. It prints the widest features on a chip and much of a package. The even older g-line sits at 436 nanometers.
why: i-line is the one tier where a Chinese toolmaker has a measurable share, about 4 percent of the world market, and nothing above it.

aka: scanners, stepper, steppers, lithography scanner, lithography scanners, lithography machine, lithography system, lithography systems
plain: A scanner is the lithography machine itself: it holds the photomask up to a light source and projects a shrunken image of one layer onto the wafer, sweeping mask and wafer past each other in a narrow slit of light. An older stepper exposes the whole field at once instead of scanning. One EUV scanner costs about $200 million.
why: ASML makes every EUV scanner in the world, so the scanner is the tool most of the export-control story is about.

aka: plasmas, plasma etch, plasma-enhanced, plasma source
plain: A plasma is a gas that has had electrons knocked off its atoms by an electric field, leaving charged fragments that react with whatever they touch. Most deposition and etch happens in a plasma inside a vacuum chamber, and the extreme ultraviolet light source is a plasma of vaporized tin.
why: Change the gas, pressure and power in the chamber and the same plasma tool either adds a film or removes one, which is why export rules name process recipes.

aka: electron-beam, e-beam, electron beams, multi-beam, multibeam, e-beam inspection, electron-beam metrology
plain: An electron beam is a stream of electrons focused to a spot far smaller than any spot of light. Fabs use it to write the pattern onto a photomask, to inspect wafers for defects light cannot see, and to measure line widths. A multi-beam tool fires thousands of beams at once because a single beam is slow.
why: Only two firms make the multi-beam writers that cut EUV masks, and the December 2024 rule controls any inspection tool using two or more beams.

aka: mask writers, multi-beam writer, multi-beam writers, electron-beam writer, e-beam writer, mask writing
plain: A mask writer is the machine that cuts a chip's pattern into a photomask blank with an electron beam, one shape at a time. A dense EUV mask carries billions of shapes, so modern writers fire many beams at once to finish in hours.
why: No new chip can be printed until its masks are written, and only IMS Nanofabrication and NuFlare make the multi-beam writers EUV masks need.

aka: mask blanks, EUV blank, EUV blanks, photomask blank, photomask blanks, blank plate, DUV blanks
plain: A mask blank is a photomask before any pattern is on it: a six-inch square of very flat glass carrying the coating the pattern will be cut into. For extreme ultraviolet the coating is a mirror of about forty pairs of ultrathin layers, and a single buried particle ruins the plate.
why: Three firms in the world make EUV blanks and one Japanese firm certifies them, on a business too small to attract a funded entrant.

aka: physical vapor deposition, sputtering, sputtering target, sputtering targets, sputter
plain: Physical vapor deposition, or PVD, coats a wafer by knocking atoms off a solid slab of metal, the sputtering target, in a vacuum so they fly across and land on the wafer as a thin film. It lays down the metal barriers and seed layers under a chip's copper wiring.
why: Every copper wire needs that barrier, because copper seeps into the insulator around it. JX Advanced Metals supplies about 65 percent of the world's sputtering targets.

aka: chemical vapor deposition, PECVD, plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition, MOCVD, CVD precursor, precursor, precursors
plain: Chemical vapor deposition, or CVD, grows a film by flowing gases over a hot wafer so they react on its surface and leave a solid layer behind. The plasma-enhanced version, PECVD, runs cooler. The gases used are called precursors.
why: Along with etch, CVD is the volume business of a fab and the segment where Chinese toolmakers have gained most.

aka: dielectrics, dielectric etch, dielectric properties, insulator, insulating layer
plain: A dielectric is an insulator: a material that does not conduct, such as the glassy oxides and nitrides between a chip's wires or the epoxy in a package substrate. Dielectric etch cuts holes and trenches through those insulating layers so the wires can be laid in.
why: How much signal a dielectric absorbs sets how fast a substrate or circuit board can run, which is why laminate suppliers matter to AI systems.

aka: critical dimensions, CD, CD-SEM, critical-dimension, line width, line-width, line widths
plain: The critical dimension is the width of the finest printed feature on a layer, the number a lithography and etch step is judged by. A CD-SEM is an electron microscope built to measure it across a wafer without cutting anything.
why: It is how a fab tells whether each lithography and etch step came out the right width. Hitachi holds 71.9 percent of the tools that measure it, the one kind Japan leads.

aka: backside power, backside vias, PowerVia, Super Power Rail, backside power network
plain: Backside power delivery grinds a finished wafer thin and builds the wires that carry power on its underside, so the wiring above the transistors carries only signals. Power arrives through holes drilled up from below, clear of the crowded top.
why: Intel ships it on 18A and TSMC on A16; it is one of the few remaining ways to make a chip faster without shrinking the transistor.

aka: copper vias, vertical vias, vertical copper vias
plain: Vias are the small vertical holes, filled with metal, that connect one layer of wiring to the layer above or below it. A chip has billions; an interposer has them through its whole thickness; a package substrate has them drilled by laser through each sheet of film.
why: Every added layer is another set of vias that can fail, which is why yield falls as packages and substrates grow.

aka: coater-developer, coater and developer, coater/developer track, track tool, track tools
plain: A coater/developer, or track, is the machine that spins a thin coat of photoresist onto the wafer before it enters the scanner and washes away the exposed parts after it comes out. It is bolted to the scanner and every layer passes through it twice.
why: No pattern can be printed without it, and one firm, Tokyo Electron, holds 91 percent of the market, one of the highest shares in the tool industry.

aka: lots, wafer lot, wafer lots, per lot
plain: A lot is the batch of wafers a fab moves through its machines together, usually 25 in one sealed carrier. Recipes, inspections and yield are tracked lot by lot.
why: How many wafers per lot a fab can afford to inspect is a cost decision that sets what process control costs it.

aka: front end of line, FEOL, front-end, front-end wafers
plain: The front end of line is the first half of making a chip, the steps that build the transistors in the silicon. In the industry at large, the front end means the whole wafer fab, as against the back end where chips are packaged and tested.
why: By 2026 front-end wafers had overtaken packaging as the tightest constraint on AI chip output.

aka: back end of line, BEOL, back-end, back-end fabs, back-end tools
plain: Inside a fab, the back end of line is the second half of making a chip, the dozen or more layers of copper wiring stacked above the transistors. In the industry at large, the back end means everything after the wafer leaves the fab: grinding, dicing, packaging and test.
why: Wiring is now as hard as the transistor, and the back end is the part of the chain where China is closest to self-sufficiency.

aka: static random-access memory, cache, on-chip memory, on-die SRAM, on-die memory, L2 cache
plain: SRAM is the fast memory built from transistors on the logic chip itself, used as a cache that holds the numbers a processor is about to need. It is far faster than the memory stacks beside the chip and far smaller, because each bit takes six transistors.
why: The SRAM cell has stopped shrinking with each node, which caps how much cache an accelerator can carry and pushes memory off the die into HBM.

aka: HVM, volume production, mass production, high volume, in volume, production ramp
plain: High-volume manufacturing is the point where a new process or product stops being a trial and runs at full rate with enough good chips to sell. A process reaches it a year or more after its first working wafers.
why: Announcements name the year a node enters high-volume manufacturing; until then a process exists only on pilot lines.

aka: ramps, ramp-up, ramping, yield at ramp
plain: A ramp is the months in which a new process or product climbs from a few wafers a week to full output while the share of working chips rises. Yield is lowest at the start of the ramp and improves as engineers find which steps lose dies.
why: Yield at ramp separates a profitable node from a subsidized one, and Intel Foundry's losses come from the ramp.

aka: thermocompression, thermo-compression bonding, thermocompression bonder, thermocompression bonders, TCB, die bonder, die bonders, bonder, bonders
plain: Thermocompression bonding presses one die onto another, or onto a substrate, under heat and force until the tiny solder bumps between them melt and join. It is how memory dies are stacked into an HBM cube and how chiplets are placed on a package.
why: The bonders place one die at a time, three or four firms make them, and ASMPT's line grew 146 percent in 2025 on AI demand.

aka: wafer dicing, dicing saw, dicing saws, grinding, wafer grinding, grinders, wafer grinders, thinning, wafer thinning
plain: Dicing cuts a finished wafer into its individual dies with a diamond saw or a laser. Grinding, done first, thins the wafer from the back, sometimes until it is a few hundredths of a millimeter thick so it can be stacked.
why: HBM depends on the grinding, which thins each memory die to about 30 micrometers so its copper columns come through. Disco of Japan leads in both steps.

aka: panel-level, panel level packaging, rectangular panel, rectangular panels
plain: Panel-level packaging builds packages on a large rectangular sheet instead of a round wafer, so far less area is wasted at the edges and many more packages fit on one carrier. It is the industry's way around the size limits of a 300 mm wafer.
why: The first panel-level line for AI chips is due in 2027, which would ease the CoWoS bottleneck.

aka: wafer test, probe test, wafer probe
plain: Wafer sort is the first test a chip gets, while it is still on the wafer. A probe card lowers thousands of needles onto the pads of one die, a tester drives signals in and reads the answers, and any die that answers wrong is marked and never packaged.
why: Proving a die good before it is packaged now saves the eight memory stacks and the substrate that a bad die would otherwise waste.

aka: burn in, wafer-level burn-in, burn-in test
plain: Burn-in runs a chip hot and under power for hours so that anything that would have failed in its first months fails now, before the part is shipped. It used to happen after packaging; for AI chips it is moving back onto the wafer.
why: One weak die in a package of a dozen expensive parts scraps all of them, so burn-in now protects everything else in the package.

aka: qualify, qualifies, qualified, qualifying, requalify, requalification, qualification tests, qualification lock-in
plain: Qualification is the months of testing a fab or a customer runs before it will accept a new material, tool or supplier for one product. A resist, a slurry, a wafer source or a memory stack is approved for one layer of one product at one fab, and switching means running the whole test again.
why: Qualification, counted in quarters, is what makes a second source slow, and it protects every incumbent in this chain.

aka: second sources, second-source, multi-sourcing, dual source, single source, sole source, single-source
plain: A second source is a second supplier qualified for the same part or material, so that a fab can keep running if the first one stops shipping. A single-source part has none, and adding one means joint development and a fresh qualification.
why: Every disruption in this chain so far has been absorbed within a year, and each one added a second source somewhere.

aka: mask shops, mask making, mask maker, mask makers
plain: A mask shop is the factory, inside a foundry or run by a specialist such as Photronics, that turns a finished chip design into its set of photomasks. It writes each plate with an electron beam, inspects it and repairs it.
why: TSMC, Samsung and Intel run their own to control turnaround time, and a fab without its mask shops nearby is not a substitute for one that has them.

aka: silicon IP, IP blocks, licensed blocks, licensed circuit blocks, semiconductor IP, IP catalog, intellectual property
plain: In chip design, IP means a ready-made block of circuitry, such as a processor core or a memory interface, that a design house licenses. Arm sells processor IP; others sell the blocks that talk to memory, PCIe or another chiplet.
why: Each licensed block must be proven on a new process before a chip can use it, and the memory interface is the hardest to buy.

aka: register-transfer level, register-transfer-level, register transfer level, RTL description, RTL code
plain: RTL, for register-transfer level, is the code in which a chip is first written: a text description, in a language such as SystemVerilog, of what every storage element holds on every tick of the clock. Software later turns it into transistors and wires.
why: It fixes what the chip does, so the largest team on most projects checks it, since a mistake found after tape-out costs a new mask set.

aka: sign-off, static timing analysis, timing signoff, timing sign-off, physical verification, signed off
plain: Signoff is the final set of automated checks a chip design must pass before a foundry will make it: that every signal arrives in time at the clock speed promised, and that every shape in the layout can be printed. Static timing analysis is the timing half; physical verification is the layout half.
why: Synopsys holds more than 90 percent of timing signoff and Siemens 85 percent of physical verification, and a foundry accepts no design that has not passed them.

aka: process design kit, process design kits
plain: A process design kit, or PDK, is the file set a foundry gives designers describing exactly what its factory can print: the sizes, spacings and electrical behavior of every feature on one node. Design software is checked against it before a chip is accepted.
why: A PDK is written against specific tool versions, which is why a design team cannot mix vendors' software.

aka: RISC-V cores, RISC-V processor
plain: RISC-V is an open instruction set, the list of basic commands a processor understands, that anyone may use without a license. Companies build their own processor cores on it, and Nvidia now uses such cores for housekeeping inside every GPU.
why: It is the license-free alternative to Arm, and Chinese designers are adopting it to end their dependence on foreign firms for processor cores.

aka: PCI Express, PCIe 6, PCIe 7
plain: PCIe is the standard connector and link that joins a processor to the cards inside a computer, an accelerator included. Each generation doubles the speed. In an AI server it carries data between the host processor and the GPUs, while faster private links join the GPUs to each other.
why: The PCIe block is licensed IP that has to be proven on each new node before a chip can use it.

aka: Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express, UCIe 3.0
plain: UCIe is an open standard for the short, very fast link between two chiplets sitting side by side in one package. It lets chiplets from different vendors be wired together, the way PCIe lets cards from different vendors share a computer.
why: Accelerators too large to print as one chip are built from chiplets, and a shared standard lets more firms supply the pieces.

aka: serializer-deserializer, high-speed serial links, serial links, serial link
plain: A SerDes, for serializer-deserializer, is the circuit at the edge of a chip that turns many slow parallel signals into one very fast stream over a single wire, and back again at the other end. Every link out of an accelerator, to another chip, a switch or an optical module, runs through one.
why: SerDes speed sets how much data a chip can move, and the blocks are licensed IP that few firms can design at the leading edge.

aka: microbumps, solder bump, solder bumps, bumps, bump, bump metrology
plain: A microbump is a dot of solder, a few hundredths of a millimeter across, that joins a die to the interposer or substrate beneath it. A large chip has tens of thousands, spaced 30 to 40 microns apart, and each one is an electrical connection that has to survive the package heating and cooling.
why: Their spacing limits how many connections fit between stacked or neighboring chips. Hybrid bonding, copper pressed straight onto copper, would pack them far closer, and it is not yet ready for HBM.

aka: RDL, redistribution wiring, redistribution layers
plain: A redistribution layer is a thin sheet of fine copper wiring, laid down in resin, that spreads a die's tightly spaced connections out to a wider pattern the package can handle. CoWoS-R and CoWoS-L use it in place of a full silicon interposer.
why: Swapping silicon for redistribution wiring is how TSMC pushed packages past 3.3 times the reticle size.

aka: silicon bridges, EMIB, silicon-bridge, local silicon bridges, embedded bridge
plain: A silicon bridge is a small sliver of silicon carrying dense wiring, set into the package only where two dies need thousands of connections between them, so the rest of the package can use cheaper wiring. Intel calls its version EMIB; TSMC's CoWoS-L uses the same idea.
why: Bridges let a package grow past a single interposer's size limit, which is how CoWoS-L carries Blackwell and Rubin. Placing them went badly on the first Blackwell packages.

aka: PCB, PCBs, printed circuit boards, circuit board, circuit boards, high-multilayer PCB
plain: A printed circuit board is the flat green or black card that electronic parts are soldered onto, with its wiring etched from copper sheets and stacked in layers. The board under an AI GPU has more than 30 layers and carries hundreds of amps.
why: It carries the power and the links between GPUs, and how much signal its laminate absorbs is now a main design limit.

aka: laminates, copper-clad laminate, copper-clad laminates, low-loss laminate, core laminate
plain: A laminate is a stiff sheet made by pressing glass cloth and resin together, usually with copper foil bonded to its faces. It is the material a circuit board or a substrate core is cut from. A low-loss laminate absorbs little of the signal passing through the wires on it.
why: How much signal the laminate absorbs has become a main design limit on the boards that link GPUs.

aka: T-glass, low-expansion glass, glass fiber cloth, low-expansion glass cloth
plain: Glass cloth is a woven fabric of fine glass fibers that gives a substrate core or circuit board its stiffness. T-glass is a special grade that barely expands when heated, which keeps a large package flat.
why: One Japanese company, Nitto Boseki, supplies the low-expansion cloth under every large AI package, and its plants are running at full capacity.

aka: CTE, thermal expansion, expansion mismatch, low-CTE
plain: The coefficient of thermal expansion is how much a material swells for each degree it warms. Silicon barely moves; epoxy moves several times more. Bolt the two together, heat them, and the package bends.
why: Matching expansion across die, bridge, interposer and substrate is what warpage control means, and it gets harder as packages grow.

aka: base chip, base logic die, logic base die, HBM base die
plain: The base die is the bottom chip of an HBM stack, the one that talks to the processor on behalf of the memory dies stacked above it. From HBM4 it is a logic chip made in a foundry.
why: That change gives TSMC a share of a product it does not make, and ties HBM4 supply to foundry capacity.

aka: 3D NAND, NAND flash, flash memory, 128-layer NAND
plain: NAND is the memory that keeps data when the power is off: the storage inside a phone, a laptop drive or a data center disk. 3D NAND stacks its cells in hundreds of layers, made by etching holes far deeper than they are wide. It is slow next to DRAM and is not used inside an AI accelerator.
why: The 2022 rules set a fab threshold at 128-layer NAND, aimed at YMTC, a Chinese maker of it.

aka: JESD270-4, JEDEC standard
plain: JEDEC is the industry body that writes the standards for memory chips, so that a memory stack from any maker fits any processor built to the same specification. Its HBM4 standard, published in April 2025, sets the width and speed of the interface.
why: Nvidia's qualification bar sits above the JEDEC baseline, which is why passing the standard is not the same as winning the order.

aka: bandwidth density, bandwidth-density
plain: Memory bandwidth density is how much data a memory stack can move each second divided by its area: gigabytes per second per square millimeter. The December 2024 rule controls any stack above 2, and every HBM stack in production is far above it.
why: One threshold catches every part worth buying, which is why the HBM control works where the chip controls let parts through.

aka: baseboards, SXM, OAM, accelerator module, HGX, HGX baseboard
plain: A baseboard is the large circuit board that eight accelerator modules bolt onto inside a server, carrying their power and the switch chips that let them reach each other at full speed. Nvidia's module is called SXM and its baseboard HGX; the open-standard equivalents are OAM and UBB.
why: Rack-scale systems such as the NVL72 have no baseboard and wire 72 GPUs together directly.

aka: Quantum-2, Quantum-X800
plain: InfiniBand is a networking standard built for supercomputers, with low delay and no dropped packets, that AI clusters used to link thousands of servers before Ethernet caught up. Nvidia owns the main supplier and sells both.
why: The choice between InfiniBand and Ethernet decides who sells the switch chips, and Broadcom's Ethernet parts now double in bandwidth every generation.

aka: Ultra Ethernet, Spectrum-X, Spectrum-X Ethernet, Tomahawk, Ethernet switch
plain: Ethernet is the ordinary networking standard of offices and the internet, now made fast and reliable enough to link the servers of an AI cluster. The switch chips at its heart, such as Broadcom's Tomahawk, route traffic between thousands of accelerators.
why: Ethernet took the scale-out layer back from InfiniBand on raw capacity, and Broadcom sells the chips to everyone.

aka: co-packaged, co-packaging, CPO, plug-in modules, plug-in optics
plain: Co-packaged optics puts the lasers and light-to-electricity converters onto the switch chip's own package instead of into plug-in modules at the front of the box. The electrical path shrinks from centimeters to millimeters, which cuts the power the optics burn by about 70 percent.
why: Optics dominate network power at 800 gigabits and above, so both switch vendors are moving to it during 2026.

aka: InP, indium
plain: Indium phosphide is a crystal, grown from the metal indium and phosphorus, that gives off light when current passes through it, which silicon cannot do. It is the material of the lasers inside the fastest optical modules. Indium itself is recovered as a byproduct of zinc mining.
why: China produces about 70 percent of the world's indium, and Nvidia paid $4 billion for laser capacity it could not simply order.

aka: busbars, copper busbar, copper busbars
plain: A busbar is a thick bar of solid copper that carries very large currents down the back of a rack to the boards that need them, doing the job a cable would melt trying to do. The bar feeding one AI rack weighs about 200 kilograms.
why: Nvidia's move to 800-volt distribution exists to push more power through the same copper and retire those bars.

aka: power shelves, rack power shelf
plain: A power shelf is a slide-in unit in a rack that converts the incoming supply to the voltage the boards use and feeds it to the busbar. A GB300 NVL72 rack draws its 142 kilowatts through eight of them at 33 kilowatts each.
why: The shelves and the boards behind them have many suppliers; the transformers upstream do not.

aka: large power transformers, transformer, transformers, switchgear, substation
plain: A large power transformer is the machine, the size of a house, that steps grid electricity down from transmission voltage to a level a data center can use. Switchgear is the heavy switching and protection equipment around it, and together they make up the substation at the gate of the campus.
why: A transformer ordered today arrives in about three years, against under a year before 2020, and that queue is where AI buildouts slip.

aka: square millimeters, square millimeter, mm²
plain: mm2 means square millimeters, the unit chip areas are given in. A lithography scanner prints at most 858 mm2 in one shot, an AI GPU die is about 800 mm2, and the largest planned interposer is 12,000 mm2, about the area of a compact disc.
why: Yield falls faster than area rises, so mm2 is the number behind most of what a chip costs.

aka: kW, kilowatts, megawatt, MW, megawatts, gigawatt, GW, gigawatts
plain: A kilowatt is a thousand watts, about what a hair dryer draws. A megawatt is a thousand kilowatts, a gigawatt a thousand megawatts, roughly the output of one large power station. One AI rack draws 142 kilowatts; a data center campus is now sized in gigawatts.
why: A gigawatt of accelerators is what OpenAI and Broadcom mean when they announce a deal, and power is what limits it.

aka: terawatt-hour, terawatt-hours, terawatt hours
plain: A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours, the unit national electricity use is counted in. US data centers used 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4 percent of the country's electricity.
why: The projection of 325 to 580 TWh by 2028 is the number the grid debate turns on.

aka: TB/s, Gb/s, Tbps, gigabytes per second, terabytes per second, gigabits per second, terabits per second
