plain: GB/s is gigabytes per second, the measure of how much data a link or a memory can move; TB/s is a thousand times more. A lowercase b, as in Gb/s or Tbps, counts bits, each an eighth of a byte. One HBM stack moves over 2 TB/s; NVLink 6 gives each GPU 3,600 GB/s.
why: The first US chip rule caught any part with a 600 GB/s link, and the 2026 rule sets a 6,500 GB/s memory ceiling.

aka: wafers a month, wafer starts, wafer starts per month, WSPM, wafer starts a month, million wafers per month
plain: Wafers per month is how fab capacity is counted: the number of wafers a plant can start through its line each month. A TSMC gigafab runs more than 100,000; SMIC's advanced lines run about 45,000. Figures are often converted to 8-inch or 12-inch equivalents so plants with different wafer sizes can be compared.
why: China leads the world in wafers per month and almost none of it is advanced, and that gap is what the contest is about.

aka: 300-millimeter, 12-inch, 12-inch equivalent, 200 mm, 8-inch, 8-inch-equivalent, 450 mm, 150 mm
plain: 300 mm is the diameter of the standard wafer, about twelve inches. Older fabs run 200 mm, or 8-inch, wafers, which carry less than half as many chips. The industry has stayed at 300 mm since 2002 and abandoned the move to 450 mm.
why: Every leading-edge chip is made on 300 mm, and 300 mm wafers carry 99.7 percent of capacity at 45 nm and below.

aka: nm, nanometers, microns, micrometer, micrometers, angstrom, angstroms, picometer, picometers
plain: A nanometer is a billionth of a meter, about the width of ten atoms; a human hair is about 80,000 of them across. A micron, or micrometer, is a thousand nanometers, an angstrom is a tenth of a nanometer, and a picometer is a thousandth. Lithography light is measured in nanometers, package bumps in microns, and mirror flatness in picometers.
why: Node names such as 2 nm no longer describe any feature that size, but the physical limits of printing and stacking are still set in these units.

aka: pitches, half-pitch, gate pitch, metal pitch, wire pitch, line pitch
plain: Pitch is the distance from one line on a chip to the next, center to center, so it counts the line and the gap together. Half-pitch is half that. A 16 nm pitch means lines 16 nanometers apart; the 2022 rules set a DRAM threshold at 18 nm half-pitch.
why: Pitch is the reliable measure of how fine a process prints.

aka: 5 nm-class, 7 nm-class, 2 nm-class, nanometer-class, nm class
plain: Nm-class, as in 7 nm-class, means a process roughly as dense as the foundries' 7 nm generation, used when a maker's own name for the node is different or when nothing on it measures 7 nanometers. Node names stopped describing a physical size around 2010.
why: SMIC's 7 nm-class and 5 nm-class processes, made without EUV, are the ceiling on China's own AI chips.

aka: logic density, chip density, transistors per square millimeter, density gain
plain: Transistor density is how many transistors fit in a square millimeter of chip, now over 100 million on a leading-edge logic process. Each new node has traditionally raised it by a large step; the step is now about 1.1 to 1.2 times.
why: No foundry publishes wafer prices, so the shrinking density gain per node is the only public proxy for cost per transistor, and it says cost is rising.

aka: wafers an hour, wafers per hour, wafers-per-hour
plain: Throughput is how many wafers a machine can process in an hour. An EUV scanner reaches about 220, an inspection tool far fewer, and a bonder places one die at a time.
why: Throughput sets cost per layer and decides how many wafers a fab can afford to inspect, which is why brighter light sources and multi-beam tools matter.

aka: utilization rate, fab utilization
plain: Utilization is how full a fab's lines are running, as a share of what they could run. A fab costs the same whether it is full or empty, so utilization decides whether it makes money.
why: SMIC's 93.5 percent shows what a captive home market does for volume, and its 21 percent gross margin shows what it does not do for price.

aka: operating profit, operating loss, operating income
plain: Operating margin is what is left of revenue after both the cost of making the product and the cost of running the company, research and sales included, as a share of revenue. It sits below gross margin, which counts only the cost of making.
why: SK hynix publishes no gross margin, so its 76 percent operating margin is the number that shows where HBM profits went.

aka: lead times, delivery time
plain: Lead time is the wait between placing an order and receiving it. A wafer clears a fab in months; a large power transformer ordered today takes about three years, and six years of gas turbine output is already sold.
why: Money buys silicon capacity faster than it buys power capacity, and lead time is where that difference shows.

aka: oligopolies, duopoly, three-firm oligopoly
plain: An oligopoly is a market with only a few sellers, so each one's decisions move the price; a duopoly has two. DRAM, industrial gases, substrates and chip testers are all oligopolies.
why: Most stages of this chain are oligopolies, a few are monopolies, and the difference decides whether losing one supplier stops the line.

aka: leading-edge, at the leading edge, advanced node, advanced nodes, advanced-node
plain: The leading edge is the newest generation of chipmaking process in volume production, today the 3 nm and 2 nm nodes, made only by TSMC, Samsung and Intel. A leading-edge chip is one built on it. Everything older is a mature node.
why: Export controls draw their line at the leading edge, and only TSMC runs it at volume for outside customers.

aka: mature nodes, mature-node, mature logic, older nodes, older lines, trailing edge
plain: A mature node is an older chipmaking process, 28 nm and above, that has run for years and competes on price. Most of the world's wafers come off these lines, making power chips, analog parts and microcontrollers.
why: China holds about 38 percent of mature logic capacity and is moving to domestic suppliers there on a visible timetable, while the leading edge stays out of reach.

aka: original design manufacturer, ODMs, contract manufacturer, contract manufacturers, contract manufacturing, EMS, server ODM
plain: An ODM, for original design manufacturer, is a firm such as Foxconn, Quanta or Wistron that designs and builds servers and racks to a customer's specification and puts the customer's name on the box. A contract manufacturer does the assembly only.
why: Several ODMs on three continents can build an AI rack, which is why rack integration earns low-teens margins and is not a chokepoint.

aka: inference chip, inference chips, inference accelerator, inference accelerators, training and inference
plain: Running a finished AI model to answer requests, such as a prompt. Training, a run of weeks on a cluster of accelerators, builds the model first. To write each word of an answer, the chip reads the whole model from memory, does a little arithmetic and waits for the next read. Training reuses each number it fetches, so it fetches little and computes a lot.
why: Inference is where memory size and speed set how many people one chip can serve, which is why HBM decides how fast a GPU runs.

aka: weights, frontier model weights, trained weights
plain: Model weights are the billions of numbers an AI model consists of once it has been trained, the file that runs on the chips. Copy the weights and the model goes with them.
why: A chip reads every weight from memory for each word it writes, so bigger models need more HBM. The AI Diffusion rule made frontier weights a controlled item, ECCN 4E091, reaching past the chips to what they produce.

aka: export controls, export licensing, export license, export licenses, export licence, export licences, export-control
plain: An export control is a rule that makes a sale need the government's permission. The government names an item and a buyer, and from then on its own companies must hold a license before they ship that item to that buyer. The United States stretches the rule to goods made abroad with American technology.
why: It works only when the seller's firms make something the buyer cannot get elsewhere, and each chapter tests that condition for one stage of the chain.

plain: 3A090 is the entry in the US export control list that covers advanced AI chips, defined by their total processing performance and performance density; 4A090 covers the computers built from them. Its part c, added in December 2024, covers high bandwidth memory. A chip inside 3A090.a needs a license for China and, since 2025, for most of the world.
why: It decides which AI chips need a license for China, so designers now build chips around its thresholds.

plain: 3B001 and 3B090 are the entries in the US export control list that cover chipmaking equipment, written as process specifications: an etch tool that cuts sideways, a deposition tool that reaches 200-to-1 holes. The related 3D and 3E entries cover the software and know-how that go with the tools.
why: They decide which chipmaking tools need an export license, and they describe what a tool can do, since the same chamber can add or remove material depending on its recipe.

aka: affiliates rule, 50 percent rule, affiliates of listed entities
plain: The Affiliates Rule extended the Entity List to any company at least half owned by a listed firm, anywhere in the world, so that a listed company could not buy through a subsidiary. It took effect on 29 September 2025 and was suspended for a year six weeks later.
why: It is stayed to 9 November 2026, and its return would reach the subsidiaries that toolmakers still sell to.

aka: US persons, U.S. person, U.S. persons
plain: In export law a US person is any American citizen, resident or company, wherever in the world they are. Since October 2022 a US person may not service or support an advanced chip fab in China without a license.
why: The rule emptied Chinese fabs of American engineers within days, and it reaches people directly.

aka: consignees, named consignee, named consignees, ultimate consignee
plain: The consignee is the party a shipment is sent to, the name on the export license. A named consignee, such as G42 in the United Arab Emirates, can receive controlled chips on the terms attached to its own name.
why: The 2026 UAE rule attaches its terms to a list of consignees, so the deal follows the buyer across borders.

aka: approval is presumed, presumed approval
plain: A presumption of approval means a license is still required but will normally be granted. It is the opposite of a presumption of denial, and the two can sit inside one rule: HBM sales into China are presumed approved for a buyer headquartered elsewhere and presumed denied for a Chinese one.
why: That split is what keeps the Chinese plants of Korean and American firms inside the trade.

aka: case by case, case-by-case, reviewed case by case
plain: Case-by-case review means a license is required and each application is judged on its own, with no presumption either way. Since January 2026 the H200 and MI325X are reviewed this way for China, with conditions attached to each approval.
why: It is the middle setting between an open market and a presumption of denial, and it is where the current settlement sits.

aka: AIA, Artificial Intelligence Authorization
plain: License Exception AIA, for Artificial Intelligence Authorization, lets the top band of AI chips ship without a license to nineteen close allies listed in the export regulations. The AI Diffusion rule created it in January 2025 as the exception inside a worldwide license requirement.
why: BIS said in May 2025 that it would not enforce the rule, but the rule was never repealed, so AIA still stands in the Code and still governs who can buy freely.

aka: ACM, Advanced Compute Manufacturing
plain: License Exception ACM, for Advanced Compute Manufacturing, lets controlled AI chips move to a foundry or packaging plant abroad for manufacturing and testing without a full license. It is a sibling of AIA and LPP.
why: Without it, every wafer moving between fab, packager and tester across a border would need its own license.

aka: AI Diffusion, diffusion rule, Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, AI Diffusion framework
plain: The AI Diffusion rule, published on 15 January 2025, required a license to ship the most capable AI chips anywhere in the world, then opened exceptions: unlimited to nineteen allies, capped volumes elsewhere, nothing to China. It also controlled the weights of frontier AI models.
why: Four months later BIS said it would leave the rule unenforced, and it withdrew none of the text, so its license requirement and exceptions still stand.

aka: FR, 89 FR, 91 FR, 88 FR, Federal Register notice
plain: The Federal Register is the US government's daily journal, where every new rule is published before it takes effect. A citation such as 89 FR 96790 means volume 89, page 96790. Export control rules appear there first, and the page number is how they are cited.
why: US export rules change by notices published there, with no act of Congress, so a chip threshold can move in a week.

aka: CFR, Code of Federal Regulations, 15 CFR 742.6, part 742, part 740, part 734, supplement no. 5 to part 740, supplement no. 5
plain: The Code of Federal Regulations is the standing text of US rules, sorted into titles and parts. Title 15 holds the Export Administration Regulations: part 734 says what is subject to them, part 740 lists the license exceptions and, in its supplement no. 5, the nineteen favored destinations, and part 742 sets the licensing policy for each control.
why: A rule that was announced in the Federal Register lives on in the CFR, which is why the unenforced Diffusion rule still binds.

aka: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry
plain: METI is Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, the ministry that writes Japan's export controls and funds its chip industry. It licensed 23 categories of chipmaking equipment in July 2023 and subsidizes Rapidus, mask-blank capacity and materials plants.
why: Japan's controls apply to every destination and name no country, and METI is the office that decides them.

aka: Ministry of Commerce, China's Ministry of Commerce
plain: MOFCOM is China's Ministry of Commerce, the ministry that writes and administers China's own export controls. Its notices put gallium, germanium, antimony and the rare earths under license and, in December 2024, banned their export to the United States.
why: Beijing's retaliation targets the raw materials, and MOFCOM is the office that signs each notice.

aka: CHIPS and Science Act, CHIPS incentives, CHIPS money, CHIPS Act grants, CHIPS authorization, CHIPS Act support, CHIPS award
plain: The CHIPS and Science Act, passed in August 2022, authorized about $52.7 billion of US federal money for chip factories at home, most of it as grants to firms building fabs and plants. By July 2025 $30.9 billion had been awarded to 19 companies, and a condition of each grant bars the recipient from expanding in China.
why: It was Washington's first tool for bringing chipmaking home. TSMC's Arizona commitment alone, at $265 billion, now exceeds the whole authorization.

aka: National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, National Integrated Circuit Fund, third chip fund, China's third chip fund
plain: The Big Fund is the nickname for China's National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, the state vehicle that puts government money into Chinese chip firms. Its third round, raised in May 2024, came to 344 billion yuan, about $47 billion.
why: Cumulative state funding since 2014 is about triple the CHIPS authorization, and it has bought a tool industry and no leading-edge node.

aka: Macao, China or Macau, China and Macau
plain: Macau is a Chinese city with its own customs territory, like Hong Kong, so goods can enter it under separate rules. US export controls name China and Macau together to close that route, and treat a firm headquartered in either the same way.
why: Every chip rule since 2022 is written for China or Macau, which is why the pair appears throughout the AI Chips page.

aka: specialty gas, electronic specialty gases, bulk gases, bulk gas, electronic gases, process gas, process gases
plain: The gases a fab uses in small amounts, each for one job, such as silane, which carries silicon into the chamber to build a film, or nitrogen trifluoride, which cleans the chamber. They arrive in cylinders by the gram. Bulk gases, such as nitrogen and oxygen, arrive by the metric ton and are usually made on the fab site.
why: Only cylinder-shipped specialty gases can be embargoed, and a single molecule such as neon can come from a handful of plants.

aka: hydrofluoric acid, HF, ultra-high-purity hydrofluoric acid, high-purity hydrogen fluoride
plain: Hydrogen fluoride is a gas that dissolves glass, and hydrofluoric acid is its solution in water. Fabs use both to strip oxide layers and clean wafers between steps, at purities of a few stray atoms in a trillion.
why: When Japan put it under license for South Korea in 2019, exports fell 88 percent and Korea spent five years building its own supply.

aka: NF3
plain: Nitrogen trifluoride is a gas that, split apart in a plasma, releases fluorine that scours the deposits off the inside of a process chamber between wafers. It is the largest-volume specialty gas in a fab.
why: Any one missing chemical stops a fab, and nitrogen trifluoride comes from a handful of plants. SK Materials of Korea is one of the specialists that make it.

aka: neon gas, semiconductor-grade neon
plain: Neon is the gas inside the lasers that give deep ultraviolet scanners their light, mixed with krypton or argon and fluorine. A fab uses it by the cylinder and cannot print without it.
why: Ukraine supplied about 70 percent of the world's neon before 2022, and the fabs kept running only because they had stockpiled since 2014.

aka: wet chemical, wet processing, wet clean, cleaning chemicals, process chemicals
plain: Wet chemicals are the liquids a wafer is dipped in or sprayed with between steps: acids that strip a layer, solvents that remove resist, and ultrapure water rinses. Wet processing is any step done in liquid.
why: Five firms held more than 60 percent of the market as of 2021, and BIS controls wet tools by how selectively they etch one material over another.

aka: gallium, germanium, antimony
plain: Gallium and germanium are metals used in chips other than silicon logic: gallium in the compound wafers behind radio parts, LEDs and lasers, germanium in fiber optics, infrared lenses and satellite solar cells. Both are recovered as byproducts, gallium from aluminum refining and germanium from zinc.
why: China refines 99 percent of the world's primary gallium and used both metals as its first retaliation against US chip rules.

aka: rare earth, rare-earth, rare earth elements, medium and heavy rare earths
plain: The rare earths are seventeen metals, from samarium to yttrium, that go into the strong magnets in motors, disk drives and wind turbines, and into some lasers and glass. They are not rare in the ground, but China does nearly all the refining.
why: Beijing put seven of them under export license in April 2025 and claimed jurisdiction over any foreign product containing 0.1 percent of its rare earths.

aka: metal-oxide resists, metal oxide resist, tin-oxide resist, metal-oxide EUV photoresist
plain: A metal-oxide resist is a photoresist built on clusters of tin and oxygen. Tin absorbs extreme ultraviolet light far better than carbon, so the resist needs fewer photons to record a pattern and prints sharper edges at the smallest sizes.
why: JSR bought its inventor, Inpria, in 2021, and a Japanese state fund then bought JSR, so the chemistry High-NA needs sits under Japanese control.

aka: HPC, HPC platform, high-performance computers
plain: High-performance computing is the industry's name for the heavy end of the market: supercomputers, AI accelerators and the server processors beside them. A foundry's HPC platform is the version of a node tuned for those chips.
why: AI has made HPC the largest customer for the newest nodes, the most film layers in a substrate and the most inspection time.

aka: chips, microchip, microchips, semiconductor chip
plain: A chip is a small rectangle of silicon, usually smaller than a fingernail, that carries a complete electronic circuit made of billions of transistors. It is cut from a wafer after the circuit has been built up on it layer by layer.
why: Everything on the site is about how these rectangles get made, and who can stop the making.
